claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
A 10–20 nm chromium or tungsten-carbide coating can be deposited onto the W phase by room-temperature physical vapor deposition before consolidation.
The ultrathin coating will inhibit atomic interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Inhibiting W–Cu interdiffusion will prevent phase separation during consolidation and service.
Inhibiting W–Cu interdiffusion will suppress interfacial void nucleation and formation during consolidation and service.
The coating will produce a stabilized, coherent W–barrier–Cu interface.
The diffusion barrier will reduce chemical-potential gradients that would otherwise drive phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Suppression of interdiffusion and void formation will enhance interfacial adhesion.
Enhanced interface integrity will create a more continuous thermal-conduction path.
The barrier-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identically processed untreated W–Cu composite.
The barrier-coated composite will maintain interface integrity during relevant heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation under the stated processing and service conditions.
The proposed coating remains applicable when the coated composite is consolidated or sintered below approximately 1000 °C in an inert atmosphere.
Accelerated thermal–irradiation cycling can assess and optimize the barrier's long-term stability.
Barrier degradation or delamination could compromise the predicted improvements in interface integrity and thermal conductivity.
